title: Measles Exposure at Philadelphia Airport Triggers Alert Amid National Surge
excerpt: A measles-infected traveler moved through five terminals at Philadelphia International Airport on Sept. 13–14, prompting exposure alerts as Pennsylvania's 2026 case count hits 792.
body:
• A traveler infected with measles passed through Philadelphia International Airport on Sept. 13–14, moving through Terminals B and F and connector areas to Terminals C, D and E between 7:25 p.m. Sunday and 12:05 a.m. Monday.
  • The airport exposure was Philadelphia's second measles alert within days, following an exposure at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia on Sept. 11 that included parts of the neonatal intensive care unit.
  • Health officials say the two events are unrelated. Anyone present during the windows should check their vaccination status and watch for symptoms through Oct. 5.
  • Pennsylvania has recorded 792 measles cases in 2026, with 155 hospitalizations and four deaths, amid a national resurgence topping 3,400 cases.

Measles — the most contagious virus known to medicine — has reached one of the country's busiest airports. Philadelphia health officials warned on Friday that a person infected with measles traveled through Philadelphia International Airport from 7:25 p.m. Sunday, Sept. 13, to 12:05 a.m. Monday, Sept. 14, moving through Terminals B and F as well as areas used to connect to Terminals C, D and E. Anyone in those areas during that window may have been exposed.

The individual was traveling through Philadelphia and did not leave the airport, officials said — but that offers limited comfort with measles, which can linger in the air for up to two hours after an infected person has left a room. The city health department is notifying potentially exposed travelers and urged anyone who was in the affected areas to check whether they are immune and to contact a health care provider promptly if they are not vaccinated, are unsure of their status, are an infant, are pregnant and not immune, or are immunocompromised.

Second alert in days

The airport warning landed just days after a separate measles exposure at the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia. That exposure occurred Sept. 11 in several busy parts of the hospital, including the NICU West area, the NICU West Family Lodge, the atrium and the main cafeteria. Health authorities, including the state and Philadelphia health departments and the hospital, said they are working closely to make sure potentially exposed infants receive a preventive antibody product to prevent or lessen severe disease.

Officials emphasized that the two events are not related. Still, two exposures in one week — one touching newborns in intensive care, one touching a crowded airport during a Sunday-evening travel window — underscores how easily the virus finds new ground.

"Every Philadelphian who is fully vaccinated has little to fear from the situation at CHOP and the airport. Even more importantly, every one of those people is doing their part to help protect our most vulnerable from measles."

— Dr. Palak Raval-Nelson, Philadelphia Health Commissioner

A national resurgence

Philadelphia's alerts are part of a far larger wave. Pennsylvania has recorded 792 measles cases in 2026 across 38 counties, including 155 hospitalizations and four measles-linked deaths, according to state data. Nationally, the United States has reported 3,471 measles cases this year, surpassing last year's total, with outbreaks continuing in Pennsylvania and elsewhere.

Public health officials point to a widening immunity gap. CDC data show that 92.4 percent of kindergartners received the MMR vaccine during the 2025–2026 school year, down from 95.2 percent in 2019–2020. Two doses of the MMR vaccine are about 97 percent effective against measles — but coverage below the roughly 95 percent needed for herd immunity lets the virus circulate.

Early symptoms of measles include cough, fever, and red, watery eyes, followed by a characteristic rash. In severe cases the disease can cause pneumonia, brain infection and death. Officials advised that anyone who may have been exposed at the airport and develops symptoms through Oct. 5 should contact a doctor immediately.

What travelers should know

People born before 1957 or who have already had measles are generally considered immune, officials said. Non-immune contacts of a confirmed case may still be eligible for a preventive vaccine dose or an antibody product if given soon after exposure, and health departments may recommend up to 21 days of symptom monitoring for exposed, non-immune individuals.

For the many Indian-American families who fly through Philadelphia — including students and parents traveling during the fall semester — the message from health authorities is direct rather than alarming: know your vaccination status before you travel, and if you passed through PHL that Sunday evening and are not immune, call your health provider now rather than waiting for symptoms. Fully vaccinated travelers, officials stressed, have little to fear — and their vaccination protects the infants, pregnant travelers and immunocompromised people sharing the terminal with them.
